rubric.name: Single Responder Principle

rubric.name: Radical Brevity
rubric.description: Internal emails are 5 sentences or fewer. No greetings, no sign-offs, no social padding. Two items are a sentence, not a list — bullet points only for 3+ items.

dimensions.label: Email body is 5 sentences or fewer for internal communication
No 'hope you're well', 'thanks in advance', or similar social filler
Two items are written as a sentence — bullet points only used for 3 or more items

rubric_used.coaching_notes: Derek optimizes for inbox velocity — his emails are designed to be processed in under 10 seconds. Non-negotiable: the subject line must carry the message. Will reject any draft with social pleasantries in internal emails. External emails (investors, customers) get slightly more padding but same structure.

corrections.issue: The grader is treating this criterion as primarily about technical/engineering contexts — errors, logs, code snippets. It penalized Round 1 for not having verbatim technical artifacts, but the email was about a business decision, not a technical incident. The criterion should apply to whatever the factual claim is: if you're citing an estimate, paste the estimate as data; if you're citing an error, paste the error. Round 1's '~6 weeks' and '2–3 days' inline are actually fine for a business decision email — the grader over-penalized by expecting a code block where none was warranted. Round 2's code block is better, but not because code blocks are inherently required — it's better because it makes the data scannable and unambiguous. The grader is conflating 'paste raw evidence' with 'use code block formatting' which are not the same thing.
negative_examples: Requiring a code block for every email that contains numbers or estimates
Penalizing an email for lacking verbatim log output when the email is about a business/product decision, not a technical incident
Treating '~6 weeks of platform eng time' as a prose description failure when it is a concrete data point stated as a number
corrections.clarification: The rule is: don't describe data in prose when you can show the data directly. For technical incidents, that means paste the actual error or log line. For business decisions, that means state the actual numbers and specifics rather than vague characterizations like 'it would take a long time' or 'there are many tenants affected.' Round 1 actually satisfied this for a business email — '~6 weeks', '2–3 days', 'every tenant' are data points, not prose descriptions. The grader should not require code block formatting unless the content is genuinely code, logs, or structured technical output.

corrections.issue: The grader docked Round 2 for not explicitly naming the recipient in the draft body, calling it 'slightly ambiguous.' This is not a real violation of the principle. The single responder principle is about not creating reply-all situations or sending one email to multiple people with different asks — it is not a requirement to address the recipient by name in the body. Email clients show the To: field. Docking points for the absence of a salutation-style name reference is actually penalizing the correct behavior (no social padding) under the wrong criterion.
negative_examples: Requiring the recipient's name to appear in the email body to satisfy the single responder principle
Treating the absence of 'Hi [Name]' as ambiguity about who should respond
Conflating 'no greeting' (correct per Radical Brevity) with 'unclear responder' (a Single Responder violation)
corrections.clarification: Single Responder is satisfied when: the To: field has one person, the ask is directed at one decision-maker, and there is no CC bait or reply-all setup. It has nothing to do with whether the recipient's name appears in the body. Docking for missing name reference is actually penalizing compliance with the no-social-padding rule.

rubric_snapshot.user_goals_summary: Treats email as a synchronous interrupt — every email should cost the reader the minimum possible time. Information density is maximized, social niceties are stripped, and the subject line does the heavy lifting.

rubric.name: Subject Line as Message
rubric.description: The subject line contains the core message, not just a topic label. If the entire email fits in the subject, it goes there. The body only exists for context the subject can't carry.

dimensions.label: Subject line conveys the key point or ask, not just a topic ('Deploy blocked — Redis cert' not 'Redis issue')
The email body adds context, evidence, or detail — never repeats what the subject already said
Subject is parseable in an inbox preview without opening the email

rubric.name: Raw Evidence Over Prose Description
rubric.description: Error messages, log lines, code snippets, and data are pasted directly rather than described in prose. 'The auth service is returning 403s' is worse than pasting the actual error output.

dimensions.label: Technical evidence (errors, logs, metrics) is pasted verbatim, not paraphrased
Raw evidence has at most one sentence of framing, not a paragraph of explanation
Quantitative data appears as numbers or output, not written out in sentences

negative_examples: Requiring a code block for every email that contains numbers or estimates
Penalizing an email for lacking verbatim log output when the email is about a business/product decision, not a technical incident
Treating '~6 weeks of platform eng time' as a prose description failure when it is a concrete data point stated as a number
rubric.clarification: The rule is: don't describe data in prose when you can show the data directly. For technical incidents, that means paste the actual error or log line. For business decisions, that means state the actual numbers and specifics rather than vague characterizations like 'it would take a long time' or 'there are many tenants affected.' Round 1 actually satisfied this for a business email — '~6 weeks', '2–3 days', 'every tenant' are data points, not prose descriptions. The grader should not require code block formatting unless the content is genuinely code, logs, or structured technical output.

rubric.name: Single Responder Principle
rubric.description: Every email has exactly one intended responder. If multiple people need to act, they get separate emails with different asks. Reply-all and 'everyone please' are treated as failures.

dimensions.label: The email is addressed to one person who needs to act, not a group
Does not create situations where multiple people might respond with overlapping answers
Anyone CC'd has an explicit reason stated, or is not CC'd at all

negative_examples: Requiring the recipient's name to appear in the email body to satisfy the single responder principle
Treating the absence of 'Hi [Name]' as ambiguity about who should respond
Conflating 'no greeting' (correct per Radical Brevity) with 'unclear responder' (a Single Responder violation)
rubric.clarification: Single Responder is satisfied when: the To: field has one person, the ask is directed at one decision-maker, and there is no CC bait or reply-all setup. It has nothing to do with whether the recipient's name appears in the body. Docking for missing name reference is actually penalizing compliance with the no-social-padding rule.

rubric.name: Radical Brevity
rubric.description: Internal emails are 5 sentences or fewer. No greetings, no sign-offs, no social padding. Two items are a sentence, not a list — bullet points only for 3+ items.

dimensions.label: Email body is 5 sentences or fewer for internal communication
No 'hope you're well', 'thanks in advance', or similar social filler
Two items are written as a sentence — bullet points only used for 3 or more items

rubric_snapshot.coaching_notes: Derek optimizes for inbox velocity — his emails are designed to be processed in under 10 seconds. Non-negotiable: the subject line must carry the message. Will reject any draft with social pleasantries in internal emails. External emails (investors, customers) get slightly more padding but same structure.
